---
title: "Assignment quality criteria"
date: "2026-11-10"
categories: [assignments, workflow, reproducibility, AI]
description: "What we expect from a submission when AI does the typing: the criteria with examples, and a roadmap to a reproducible project."
---

## The deal

Use AI. You may, and you are expected to, use AI assistants for code, text, and review. In exchange, the bar is very high.

Clean code, fluent prose, and a document that renders are what an AI assistant delivers in minutes. They are the floor, not what makes a submission good. What makes it good is what AI cannot do for you: choosing a method that answers the question, checking that the results are right, reading them as an economist, and owning every line.

The criteria on this page come in three tiers.

- **The floor.** The document renders without error from a clean session with the course environment. Every number, table, and figure comes from the submitted code. Every reference exists and says what you cite it for.
- **Expected.** The criteria on code, reproducibility, communication, and writing below. With today's tools there is no reason to miss any of them.
- **What makes a submission excellent.** Verification and judgment: you benchmark your results, know your data, avoid look-ahead bias, and read the results as an economist, with honest uncertainty and limitations.

## The criteria

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  const criteria = [
 {
  "category": "Code",
  "sub": "Style",
  "criterion": "Formatted by a tool",
  "description": "Code follows the tidyverse style guide (R) or PEP 8 (Python). Format it with Air (R) or Ruff (Python), both available in Positron: inconsistent spacing and indentation have no excuse.",
  "lang": "R",
  "bad": "x=mean(returns,na.rm=TRUE)\ndf %>% filter(date>as.Date(\"2020-01-01\")) %>% mutate(ret=log(price/lag(price)))",
  "good": "mean_return <- mean(returns, na.rm = TRUE)\nprices |>\n  filter(date > as.Date(\"2020-01-01\")) |>\n  mutate(ret = log(price / lag(price)))"
 },
 {
  "category": "Code",
  "sub": "Style",
  "criterion": "One toolkit per language",
  "description": "R code uses the tidyverse with the native pipe |>; Python code uses polars, as in the course. Mixing |> and %>%, pandas and polars, or base R and tidyverse for the same task is a typical trace of code pasted together from different AI answers.",
  "lang": "Python",
  "bad": "import pandas as pd\nimport polars as pl\n\nprices = pl.read_parquet(\"data/prices_daily.parquet\")\nprices_pd = prices.to_pandas()\nreturns = prices_pd.groupby(\"symbol\")[\"adjusted_close\"].pct_change()",
  "good": "returns = prices.sort(\"symbol\", \"date\").with_columns(\n    ret=pl.col(\"adjusted_close\").pct_change().over(\"symbol\")\n)"
 },
 {
  "category": "Code",
  "sub": "Style",
  "criterion": "No leftovers",
  "description": "No commented-out code, unused objects, or print(), head() and glimpse() calls from development remain in the submitted document.",
  "lang": "R",
  "bad": "# fit <- lm(ret ~ mkt + smb, data = returns)\nfit2 <- lm(ret ~ mkt + smb + hml, data = returns)\nprint(fit2)  # check\nhead(returns)",
  "good": "fit_ff3 <- lm(ret ~ mkt + smb + hml, data = returns)"
 },
 {
  "category": "Code",
  "sub": "Structure",
  "criterion": "Proportionate code",
  "description": "The code is as simple as the task allows. No classes, configuration dictionaries, logging, or layers of wrapper functions for a one-off analysis. AI assistants tend to over-engineer, and every extra layer is something you must understand and defend.",
  "lang": "Python",
  "bad": "class PortfolioAnalyzer:\n    def __init__(self, returns, config=None):\n        self.returns = returns\n        self.config = config or {\"annualization\": 252}\n\n    def compute_sharpe(self):\n        factor = self.config[\"annualization\"]\n        return self.returns.mean() / self.returns.std() * factor**0.5\n\nsharpe = PortfolioAnalyzer(returns).compute_sharpe()",
  "good": "def annualized_sharpe(returns, periods_per_year=252):\n    return returns.mean() / returns.std() * periods_per_year**0.5\n\nsharpe = annualized_sharpe(returns)"
 },
 {
  "category": "Code",
  "sub": "Structure",
  "criterion": "No repetition",
  "description": "Logic that appears more than twice becomes a named function; the same block is never copied with small changes.",
  "lang": "R",
  "bad": "sharpe_a <- mean(returns_a) / sd(returns_a) * sqrt(252)\nsharpe_b <- mean(returns_b) / sd(returns_b) * sqrt(252)\nsharpe_c <- mean(returns_c) / sd(returns_c) * sqrt(252)",
  "good": "annualized_sharpe <- function(x) mean(x) / sd(x) * sqrt(252)\n\nreturns |>\n  group_by(portfolio) |>\n  summarize(sharpe = annualized_sharpe(ret))"
 },
 {
  "category": "Code",
  "sub": "Structure",
  "criterion": "Logical order",
  "description": "The document runs top to bottom: packages and parameters, data, cleaning, analysis, output. No chunk uses an object that a later chunk creates.",
  "lang": "R",
  "bad": "# Results section\nfit <- lm(ret ~ beta, data = returns_with_beta)  # created ten chunks later",
  "good": "# 1. Packages and parameters\n# 2. Data\n# 3. Cleaning and merging\n# 4. Beta estimation\n# 5. Cross-sectional regressions\n# 6. Tables and figures"
 },
 {
  "category": "Code",
  "sub": "Naming",
  "criterion": "Meaningful names",
  "description": "Objects and functions have names that say what they contain or do, without a comment.",

  "bad": "df2 <- df |> filter(!is.na(x))\ntmp <- lm(y ~ x + z, data = df2)",

 {

  "bad": "portfolio_vol <- sd(returns) * sqrt(252)\nrolling_mean <- slider::slide_dbl(returns, mean, .before = 21)",

 },
 {
  "category": "Code",
  "sub": "Naming",
  "criterion": "Comments explain why",
  "description": "Comments say why a step is there or why it is done this way, not what the next line does. AI-generated code narrates every line; delete those comments and keep the ones a reader needs.",
  "lang": "R",
  "bad": "# Load the data\nprices <- read_parquet(\"data/prices_daily.parquet\")\n# Compute returns\nreturns <- prices |> mutate(ret = adjusted_close / lag(adjusted_close) - 1)",
  "good": "prices <- read_parquet(\"data/prices_daily.parquet\")\n# Adjusted prices, so that returns include dividends and ignore splits\nreturns <- prices |> mutate(ret = adjusted_close / lag(adjusted_close) - 1)"

 {
  "category": "Code",
  "sub": "Robustness",
  "criterion": "Errors are not hidden",
  "description": "No tryCatch(), try/except, or suppressWarnings() that silently swallows problems, and no fallback that quietly turns a failed step into NA or zero. A step that can fail should fail loudly; a warning you have not investigated is a bug you have not found.",
  "lang": "R",
  "bad": "beta <- tryCatch(\n  coef(lm(ret_excess ~ mkt_excess, data = window))[2],\n  error = function(e) NA\n)",
  "good": "# Rule from Section 2: at least 24 monthly returns per estimation window\nestimate_beta <- function(window) {\n  if (nrow(window) < min_observations) return(NA_real_)\n  coef(lm(ret_excess ~ mkt_excess, data = window))[2]\n}"
 },
 {
  "category": "Reproducibility",
  "sub": "Execution",
  "criterion": "Renders from a clean session",

 {

  "sub": "Execution",

 },
 {

  "sub": "Results",

 },

 },
 {

  "sub": "Results",
  "criterion": "Findings discussed",

  "bad": "The regression results are presented in Table 2.",
  "good": "Table 2 shows a market beta of 0.94 (t = 12.3). The size loading is small and insignificant (0.08, t = 1.1): the portfolio has no meaningful size tilt."
 },
 {
  "category": "Communication",
  "sub": "Results",
  "criterion": "Choices are explained",

  "bad": "We use the Fama-French three-factor model.",
  "good": "We use the Fama-French three-factor model because the strategy tilts toward small value stocks, and the size and value factors capture exactly these exposures (Fama and French, 1993)."
 },
 {
  "category": "Communication",
  "sub": "Structure",
  "criterion": "Concise",
  "description": "Every paragraph earns its place within the page limit. AI makes text cheap; we value the shortest version that says everything.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "In this section, we will now turn to the analysis of the results that we have obtained from the estimation procedure described in the previous section.",
  "good": "Table 3 reports the estimates."
 },
 {
  "category": "Communication",
  "sub": "Structure",
  "criterion": "Cross-references, no placeholders",
  "description": "Figures, tables, and sections are referenced with labels (@fig-..., @tbl-..., @sec-...). No TODO, ??, or template text remains.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "The results are shown in Figure ?? and discussed in Section 4 (TODO: update).",
  "good": "@fig-rolling-sharpe shows the results, and @sec-robustness discusses them."
 },
 {
  "category": "Writing",
  "sub": "Mechanics",
  "criterion": "No spelling or grammar errors",
  "description": "With today's tools there is no excuse, so we do not overlook them.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "The portfolo is rebalenced annualy using markert capitalisation weights.",
  "good": "The portfolio is rebalanced annually using market capitalization weights."
 },
 {
  "category": "Writing",
  "sub": "Mechanics",
  "criterion": "Formal register",
  "description": "Academic register throughout: no contractions, colloquialisms, or vague quantifiers.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "The results are basically what you'd expect, and there's a lot of variation.",
  "good": "The results are consistent with the literature; the cross-sectional dispersion of returns limits their precision."
 },
 {
  "category": "Writing",
  "sub": "Mechanics",
  "criterion": "Active voice, present tense",
  "description": "Write \"we estimate\", not \"it was estimated\", and keep the present tense for methods and results.",
  "lang": "prose",

  "good": "We estimate the model by OLS. The Sharpe ratio improves from 0.41 to 0.67."
 },
 {
  "category": "Writing",
  "sub": "Precision",
  "criterion": "Precise quantitative language",

  "lang": "prose",

  "criterion": "No undefined acronyms or notation",

  "bad": "We report NW standard errors. The weight is $w_i = \\sigma_i^{-2} / \\sum_j \\sigma_j^{-2}$.",
  "good": "We report Newey-West (NW) standard errors. The weight of asset $i$ is $w_i = \\sigma_i^{-2} / \\sum_j \\sigma_j^{-2}$, where $\\sigma_i^2$ is its estimated return variance."
 },

  "sub": "Citations",
  "criterion": "Claims are cited",

  "bad": "The momentum premium is well documented and amounts to roughly 1% per month.",
  "good": "The momentum premium is well documented and amounts to roughly 1% per month (Jegadeesh and Titman, 1993)."

  "good": "@Fama1970 and @Fama1993 both argue ..."

  "category": "Verification",
  "sub": "Checks",
  "criterion": "Benchmark first",
  "description": "Before you extend an analysis, reproduce a known number: a result from the lecture, the Tidy Finance book, or the paper you follow. If you cannot match it, say so and explain the gap.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "We implement the momentum strategy and find a premium of 2.3% per month.",
  "good": "For 1965-1989, our momentum portfolio earns close to the premium in Table 1 of Jegadeesh and Titman (1993). We then extend the sample to 2025."

  "category": "Verification",
  "sub": "Checks",
  "criterion": "You know your data",
  "description": "Check observations, date range, missing values, duplicates, units (percent or decimals?), and outliers, and state the checks that matter in a sentence or two.",
  "lang": "R",
  "bad": "returns <- read_parquet(\"data/crsp_monthly.parquet\")\n# straight to the regressions",
  "good": "returns |>\n  summarize(\n    observations = n(),\n    first_month = min(date),\n    last_month = max(date),\n    missing_returns = sum(is.na(ret)),\n    duplicates = sum(duplicated(pick(permno, date))),\n    largest_abs_return = max(abs(ret), na.rm = TRUE)\n  )"
 },
 {
  "category": "Verification",
  "sub": "Checks",
  "criterion": "No look-ahead",
  "description": "Every signal, weight, and model uses only information available at the time of the decision: lag characteristics and market capitalization, and never use test data for tuning or variable selection. The code runs either way, which is why AI assistants get this wrong so easily.",
  "lang": "R",
  "bad": "portfolios <- crsp |>\n  group_by(date) |>\n  mutate(weight = mktcap / sum(mktcap))  # this month's market cap",
  "good": "portfolios <- crsp |>\n  group_by(date) |>\n  mutate(weight = mktcap_lag / sum(mktcap_lag))  # known at the start of the month"

  "category": "Verification",
  "sub": "Judgment",
  "criterion": "Read results as an economist",
  "description": "Ask whether a result is plausible in size, what mechanism could explain it, and whether it survives transaction costs. A Sharpe ratio of 3 is a reason to look for a bug, not a result.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "Our machine learning portfolio achieves an annualized Sharpe ratio of 3.4, which demonstrates the power of the approach.",
  "good": "An annualized Sharpe ratio of 3.4 is implausible for a monthly equity strategy. We traced it to returns that entered the features without a lag; with lagged features, the Sharpe ratio is 0.8."
 },
 {
  "category": "Verification",
  "sub": "Judgment",
  "criterion": "Robustness and limitations",
  "description": "Results that hinge on one arbitrary choice (sample period, window length, number of portfolios) are shown to survive a reasonable alternative, or the dependence is stated. Limitations are named honestly.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "The strategy outperforms the market.",
  "good": "The strategy outperforms the market with 10 portfolios and 60-month windows; with 36-month windows, the alpha halves and becomes insignificant (t = 1.2)."
 },
 {
  "category": "Working with AI",
  "sub": "Ownership",
  "criterion": "You own every line",
  "description": "You can explain every line of code and every sentence, and why it is there. Code you cannot explain does not belong in the submission, however well it runs.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "\"The AI suggested this transformation, and it made the error go away.\"",
  "good": "\"We winsorize returns at the 1st and 99th percentiles because five delisting returns below -90% dominate the cross-sectional means.\""
 },
 {
  "category": "Working with AI",
  "sub": "Ownership",
  "criterion": "References are real",
  "description": "Every reference exists and says what you cite it for. AI assistants invent plausible papers, page numbers, and quotes; check each one at the source (journal page, DOI).",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "Smith and Jones (2019, Journal of Finance) show that momentum disappeared after 2010.\n# a paper that does not exist",
  "good": "Every entry in references.bib was checked at its DOI, and every cited claim against the paper itself."
 },
 {
  "category": "Working with AI",
  "sub": "Ownership",
  "criterion": "Current functions only",
  "description": "The code uses functions and arguments that exist in the course's package versions and raises no deprecation warnings. AI assistants often suggest outdated or invented ones.",
  "lang": "R",
  "bad": "prices <- download_data(type = \"stock_prices\", symbols = symbols)  # old tidyfinance interface",
  "good": "prices <- download_data(\n  \"Stock Prices\",\n  symbols = symbols,\n  start_date = start_date,\n  end_date = end_date\n)"
 },
 {
  "category": "Working with AI",
  "sub": "Consistency",
  "criterion": "Narrative matches output",
  "description": "Conclusions agree with the estimates: no significance claimed where p > 0.05, no positive effect where the estimate is negative, no result from an earlier run.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "The momentum strategy generates significant alpha (alpha = 0.41, t = 1.6).",
  "good": "The momentum strategy has a positive but insignificant alpha (0.41% per month, t = 1.6)."
 },
 {
  "category": "Working with AI",
  "sub": "Prose",
  "criterion": "Specific prose, no filler",
  "description": "Every sentence says something about your analysis. Delete generic openers and closers, stock phrases (\"it is important to note\", \"delve into\", \"plays a crucial role\", \"not only ... but also\"), and bold lead-ins. A sentence that would fit any report fits none.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "In today's data-driven financial landscape, it is important to note that our analysis delves into the nuanced and multifaceted relationship between risk and return.",
  "good": "Portfolios sorted on past volatility earn lower returns than the CAPM predicts: the high-minus-low alpha is -0.6% per month (t = -2.4)."
 },
 {
  "category": "Working with AI",
  "sub": "Prose",
  "criterion": "Prose, not lists",
  "description": "Arguments and findings are written as connected prose, not bullet points: lists hide how the findings relate to each other.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "The main findings are:\n- The momentum premium is positive.\n- Transaction costs reduce net returns.\n- The effect is stronger in small caps.",
  "good": "The momentum premium is positive before costs, but transaction costs absorb most of it in small caps, where spreads are widest."
 },
 {
  "category": "Working with AI",
  "sub": "Prose",
  "criterion": "One voice",
  "description": "Register, vocabulary, and style stay the same throughout, with no shifts that reveal sections written by different people or tools.",
  "lang": "prose",
  "bad": "Methods: \"We employ a cross-sectional regression framework to identify ...\"\nResults: \"So basically the beta is positive, which is what we expected.\"",
  "good": "The same precise, plain register from the introduction to the conclusion."
 }
];
  const categories = ["All"].concat(["Code", "Reproducibility", "Communication", "Writing", "Verification", "Working with AI"]);
  const root = document.getElementById("qc-root");
  let active = "All";

  function el(tag, className, text) {
    const node = document.createElement(tag);
    if (className) node.className = className;
    if (text !== undefined) node.textContent = text;
    return node;
  }

  function example(kind, label, code) {
    const box = el("div", kind);
    box.appendChild(el("div", "qc-label " + kind, label));
    const pre = el("pre");
    pre.appendChild(el("code", null, code));
    box.appendChild(pre);
    return box;
  }

  function render() {
    root.textContent = "";
    const filters = el("div", "qc-filters");
    categories.forEach(function (category) {
      const button = el("button", category === active ? "active" : null, category);
      button.type = "button";
      button.addEventListener("click", function () { active = category; render(); });
      filters.appendChild(button);
    });
    root.appendChild(filters);

    const shown = criteria.filter(function (c) { return active === "All" || c.category === active; });
    const groups = new Map();
    shown.forEach(function (c) {
      const key = c.category + " \u00b7 " + c.sub;
      if (!groups.has(key)) groups.set(key, []);
      groups.get(key).push(c);
    });
    groups.forEach(function (items, key) {
      const group = el("div", "qc-group");
      group.appendChild(el("div", "qc-group-title", key));
      items.forEach(function (c) {
        const item = el("details", "qc-item");
        const summary = el("summary");
        summary.appendChild(el("span", "qc-name", c.criterion));
        summary.appendChild(el("span", "qc-desc", c.description));
        summary.appendChild(el("span", "qc-tag", c.lang));
        item.appendChild(summary);
        const examples = el("div", "qc-examples");
        examples.appendChild(example("bad", "Problematic", c.bad));
        examples.appendChild(example("good", "Better", c.good));
        item.appendChild(examples);
        group.appendChild(item);
      });
      root.appendChild(group);
    });
    root.appendChild(el("div", "qc-count",
      shown.length + " of " + criteria.length + " criteria \u00b7 open a criterion for an example"));
  }

  render();
})();
</script>
```

## A roadmap to a reproducible submission

The test is simple. Someone else, a peer reviewer, a teaching assistant, or you a year from now, takes your submission, sets up the course environment, and gets the same document. Journals now demand exactly this: the [Review of Financial Studies](https://review-of-financial-studies.github.io/readme.html) checks every published paper against a detailed README template. An assignment needs much less: the course environment and the data are fixed, so your document only has to run on its own. Seven steps get you there.

| Step | What it means for your submission |
|---|---|
| **1. Organize** | One project folder, ideally a Git repository, with the course files at its root (`uvr.toml`, `uvr.lock`, `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, `_quarto.yml`) and data in `data/`. All paths are relative to that folder. |
| **2. Pin the software** | Use the course environment and nothing else: `uvr sync` (R) and `uv sync` (Python) install exactly the versions in the lockfiles. No installation commands in the document. |
| **3. Document the data** | In the report, state for every data source what it is, where it comes from, how you access it (a `tidyfinance` download, a file from Absalon), the sample period, and whether it may be shared. Licensed data (CRSP, Compustat) are never committed, uploaded, or shared. |
| **4. Freeze the inputs** | Fixed start and end dates in every data request. Raw downloads stored once in `data/` and read from there. A seed for everything random. |
| **5. Run from scratch** | One command produces the document: `quarto render` (or Preview in Positron) in a fresh session, after deleting caches. |
| **6. Trace every result** | Every table and figure comes from a labeled chunk, every number in the text from inline code. Nothing is copied by hand from the console. |
| **7. Verify on another machine** | We recommend this test before you submit: a teammate takes the submitted files to their own computer, runs `uvr sync` or `uv sync`, fills `data/`, and renders. Compare the key numbers. Your submission is reproducible when it works there, not when it works on your machine. |

## Let AI review your submission

AI is also a demanding reviewer. Paste the prompt below into the assistant of your choice, together with your `.qmd` and the rendered PDF. Like the Review of Financial Studies, which offers the same kind of prompt for its replication checks, we add a warning: an AI reviewer rarely says that a document is fine as it is, and it suggests changes whether or not they are needed. Use your judgment, and do not let it rewrite your submission. An AI review does not replace step 7: render your submission yourself on a second machine.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Review prompt

```text
You are a demanding referee for a master's course in empirical finance at
the University of Copenhagen. Review the attached Quarto document (.qmd) and
its rendered PDF against the course's quality criteria:
https://aef-course.ku.dk/additional-material/assignment-quality-criteria.html

Work through six categories: code, reproducibility, communication, writing,
verification, and working with AI. For each category:
1. Say whether the submission meets the criteria (yes, partly, no).
2. Quote the code lines or passages that fall short.
3. Suggest a concrete fix.

Check in particular:
- Does every number in the text come from inline code, and does it match the
  tables and figures?
- Does any step use information before it would have been available
  (look-ahead bias, test data used for tuning)?
- Do all references exist, and do they say what the text claims? List every
  reference you cannot verify.
- Would the document render on another computer from a clean session
  (paths, sample dates, seeds, packages, data files)?

End with the three changes that would improve the submission most. Do not
rewrite the submission.
```
:::
